scope: apps/admin/** + apps/web/app/admin/** + apps/web/app/gaushala-portal/** + apps/web/app/temple-portal/** + apps/api/src/routes/admin*.ts + gaushala-portal.ts + temple-portal.ts + apps/web/lib/admin-api.ts

findings.title: Temple-portal /schedule accepts client-supplied ?slug= and any TEMPLE_MANAGER can overwrite any unlinked (org-less) temple's timingInfo
findings.evidence: userCanEditTemple (lines 79-97): `async function userCanEditTemple(templeId, userId, hasManagerRole) { ... const orgId = rows[0]?.org_id; if (!orgId) return hasManagerRole; ... }` — i.e. when a temple has no org_id (legacy/unlinked), authorization collapses to the bare role flag. Schedule GET (203-222): `server.get<{ Querystring: { slug?: string } }>('/schedule', ... { const slug = request.query.slug; if (!slug) return 400; const temple = await prisma.temple.findUnique({ where: { slug }, ... }); ... }`. Schedule PATCH (224-254): `server.patch<{ Querystring: { slug?: string }; Body: unknown }>('/schedule', ... { const slug = request.query.slug; const tRow = await prisma.temple.findUnique({ where: { slug } }); ... await prisma.temple.update({ where: { slug }, ... timingInfo ... }); }`. Web page passes slug straight from the URL: apps/web/app/temple-portal/schedule/page.tsx `const s = params.get('slug') || localStorage.getItem('temple_portal_slug'); ... fetch(`/api/v1/temple-portal/schedule?slug=${encodeURIComponent(slug)}`)`.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user holding the TEMPLE_MANAGER role can enumerate temple slugs and PATCH the timingInfo of ANY temple that has no org_id. timingInfo drives the public 'Live Darshan' / 'Next Aarti' badges, so an attacker can vandalize or deface live-darshan timings across the platform, or set bogus open windows. This is horizontal privilege escalation (manager A editing manager B's temple) plus integrity tampering of public-facing content. All other temple-portal endpoints (donations, pujas, darshan) correctly scope via resolveManagerTempleId(userId) — only the schedule endpoints are vulnerable, which matches the prior audit's localization.
findings.repro: 1. Sign in as any TEMPLE_MANAGER whose own temple is irrelevant. 2. Pick any legacy temple slug T with no org_id (e.g. a temple created before the org linkage). 3. PATCH /api/v1/temple-portal/schedule?slug=T with body { regularHours: {Monday: '00:00 - 00:00'}, closedOn: 'all' }. 4. Server resolves tRow by slug, calls userCanEditTemple(T.id, userId, true) → orgId null → returns hasManagerRole=true → update succeeds. 5. Public temple page for T now shows corrupted timings.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the `if (!orgId) return hasManagerRole` legacy fallback. userCanEditTemple must return false whenever there is no org membership proving ownership — legacy unlinked temples should be migrated to an org (even a single-member org owned by their manager) or made admin-only editable. Additionally, do NOT accept the temple identity from the client query string: resolve the slug/id from request.currentUser via the manager's TempleProfile (resolveManagerTempleId already exists and is used by donations/pujas/darshan — reuse it for /schedule too).

findings.title: temple-portal /schedule web page sends credentials:'include' with NO Authorization Bearer header — broken auth forwarding (401 for real users)
findings.evidence: GET: `fetch(`/api/v1/temple-portal/schedule?slug=${encodeURIComponent(slug)}`, { credentials: 'include' })` — no headers. PATCH: `const res = await fetch(`/api/v1/temple-portal/schedule?slug=${encodeURIComponent(slug)}`, { method: 'PATCH', credentials: 'include', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: ... })` — no Authorization header. grep for useAuth/session/accessToken/token/Bearer/Authorization in the whole file returns EMPTY. Compare to every sibling temple-portal page: temple-portal/pujas `const token = session?.accessToken;`, temple-portal/donations `const token = session?.accessToken;`, temple-portal/darshan `const token = session?.accessToken;` — all send `Authorization: Bearer ${token}`. API authenticateUser only reads the Authorization header (middlewares/auth.ts:36-37 `function extractBearerToken(request) { const authHeader = request.headers.authorization; ... }`) and does NOT read the poojly_session cookie (grep for poojly_session/cookies across apps/api/src/middlewares + routes + lib = zero matches).
findings.impact: The schedule editor is the only temple-portal page that omits the Bearer token. For any real (non-demo) temple manager, authenticateUser finds no Authorization header → 401 on both GET and PATCH, so the page can never load or save ('Failed to load schedule. You may not manage this temple.' toast fires on every visit). The feature is dead in production. This is a regression hiding behind B1: because the page never authenticates correctly, B1's IDOR is only practically reachable via a direct API call with a valid Bearer token (a logged-in TEMPLE_MANAGER hitting the endpoint through any other client), not via the broken web UI. Note the page also calls a relative `/api/v1/...` path (no API_BASE_URL) while siblings use `${API_BASE_URL}/...`, so it would only work if the API were same-origin — another sign the page was never wired up correctly.
findings.repro: 1. Sign in as a real TEMPLE_MANAGER (Supabase JWT, not demo). 2. Open /temple-portal/schedule?slug=<own-temple>. 3. Browser network tab: GET /api/v1/temple-portal/schedule?slug=... returns 401 (no Authorization header sent, only cookies). 4. Form never populates; 'Failed to load schedule' toast appears. 5. Attempting Save also 401s.
findings.suggestedFix: Mirror the sibling pages: pull `const { session } = useAuth(); const token = session?.accessToken;` and send `headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` }` on both fetches (drop `credentials:'include'` or keep it alongside the header). Use `${API_BASE_URL}` for the base path. Gate the effect on `if (!token) return;`. Then, after fixing auth forwarding, fix B1 so the slug is resolved server-side rather than trusted from the URL.

findings.title: apps/web has NO Next.js middleware — /admin/** (and all portal) pages are reachable by any user; admin role is enforced only client-side via AuthGuard
findings.evidence: No apps/web/middleware.ts and no apps/web/src/middleware.ts exist (filesystem check: `ls apps/web/middleware.ts apps/web/src/middleware.ts` → No such file). admin/layout.tsx (96-100) wraps children in client AuthGuard: `export default function AdminRootLayout({ children }) { return ( <AuthGuard allowedRoles={['admin']}> <AdminLayoutInner>{children}</AdminLayoutInner> </AuthGuard> ); }`. AuthGuard.tsx (28-67) is 'use client' and does the redirect in a useEffect: `if (!isAuthenticated) { window.location.href = `/auth/login?redirect=...` } ... if (user && allowedRoles && !allowedRoles.includes(user.role)) { window.location.href = getRoleDashboardPath(user.role); }`. The admin subpages themselves mostly import AuthGuard/useAuth but rely on the layout's wrapper (e.g. approvals/page.tsx, leads, outreach, waitlist, ratings, metrics, agents import useAuth but NOT their own AuthGuard — they inherit the layout's client guard). settings/page.tsx and commissions/page.tsx import neither.
findings.impact: All 14+ admin pages (/admin, /admin/users, /admin/approvals, /admin/leads, /admin/outreach, /admin/waitlist, /admin/support, /admin/ratings, /admin/commissions, /admin/subscriptions, /admin/revenue, /admin/reports, /admin/metrics, /admin/agents, /admin/settings) are server-rendered/200 for ANY visitor — logged-out or wrong-role — because nothing blocks the request at the edge. A non-admin who hits /admin/users receives the full HTML/JS bundle (the sidebar links, the page component code) before the client useEffect runs a window.location redirect. The actual admin DATA is still protected server-side (every apps/api admin route has preHandler [authenticateUser, requireRole('admin')], verified for admin.ts, admin-ops.ts, admin-queue.ts, admin-metrics.ts, admin-leads.ts, admin-roadmap.ts, admin-subscriptions.ts, admin-agents.ts, admin-gurukuls.ts, admin-lead-conversion.ts, admin-bookings.ts, admin-temples.ts, admin-content-queue.ts, admin-donations-export.ts, marketplace-v2 marketplaceAdminRoutes, outreachAdminRoutes, whatsappBroadcastRoutes), so this is a UI-surface / information-disclosure exposure rather than a data breach: the admin nav structure, sidebar labels, and page skeletons leak to unauthenticated users, and there is a brief flash of admin chrome before the client redirect. It also means a JS-disabled or slow client sees the admin shell indefinitely. Same pattern applies to gaushala-portal/layout.tsx (allowedRoles ['gaushala_manager']) and temple-portal/layout.tsx (['temple_manager']) — all portal gating is client-only.
findings.repro: 1. Open an incognito browser (not logged in). 2. Navigate directly to https://darshya.online/admin/users. 3. Server returns 200 with the admin layout HTML (sidebar with Users/Approvals/Leads/etc. links rendered). 4. Only after hydration does AuthGuard's useEffect fire and redirect to /auth/login. 5. View page source (before JS) — admin nav labels are visible. A curl of the URL returns the shell HTML.
findings.suggestedFix: Add apps/web/middleware.ts that reads the session cookie (poojly_session) on the server, parses the user role, and returns a 401/307 redirect for /admin/** unless role === 'admin' (and equivalent for /gaushala-portal/** → gaushala_manager, /temple-portal/** → temple_manager, /astrologer-portal/** → astrologer, /wellness-portal/** → wellness_instructor, /gurukul-portal/** → appropriate role). Keep AuthGuard as the client fallback, but make the edge middleware the authoritative gate so no admin HTML/JS reaches an unauthorized request. This also fixes the same exposure on the other portals.

findings.title: apps/admin portal gated by a single shared ADMIN_DASHBOARD_TOKEN cookie with no per-user identity, rotation, or revocation; all API calls use one shared server bearer
findings.evidence: apps/admin/middleware.ts:6-33 `const COOKIE_NAME = 'darshya_admin_session'; ... const expected = process.env.ADMIN_DASHBOARD_TOKEN; ... const presented = request.cookies.get(COOKIE_NAME)?.value; if (presented === expected) { return NextResponse.next(); }` — single env value, single cookie name, plaintext `===` compare (not timing-safe). apps/admin/lib/api.ts: `export function adminApiBearer() { const bearer = process.env.ADMIN_API_BEARER ?? process.env.ADMIN_API_TOKEN; ... return bearer; }` and `adminApiHeaders() { return { 'content-type':'application/json', authorization: `Bearer ${adminApiBearer()}`, ... } }` — every server-side API call from the admin app uses the SAME static bearer for every human operator. Comment in lib/api.ts:3-5 confirms the model: 'the admin Next.js app is gated by middleware.ts (darshya_admin_session cookie comparing to ADMIN_DASHBOARD_TOKEN). Once a request reaches a route handler we trust the caller, but the API still requires its own admin token.'
findings.impact: Two compounding weaknesses. (1) Access control: anyone who learns the single ADMIN_DASHBOARD_TOKEN cookie value gets full admin-portal access; there is no concept of individual admin accounts, no per-user revocation, no rotation without changing the shared env and disrupting every operator simultaneously, and the cookie is a long-lived static secret shared by all admins. The comparison is also non-constant-time (`presented === expected`). (2) Auditability: because all API calls are made with one shared ADMIN_API_BEARER, the API cannot distinguish which human admin performed a given destructive action (role change, approval, payout, refund, content moderation, lead status flip) — every action is attributed to the same identity, defeating per-actor audit trails. This is an internal/admin-only surface so severity is LOW, but it is a real gap versus per-user authn.
findings.repro: 1. As any operator, set cookie darshya_admin_session=<ADMIN_DASHBOARD_TOKEN>. 2. Full admin portal opens. 3. Perform a destructive action (e.g. approve a provider, change a user's role). 4. API logs show the actor as the single shared admin bearer, not the individual — no way to tell which operator did it. 5. To revoke one compromised operator you must rotate ADMIN_DASHBOARD_TOKEN, kicking out every other admin too.
findings.suggestedFix: Move apps/admin to per-user auth (reuse the same Supabase JWT + role system as apps/web) and add apps/admin/middleware.ts that verifies a real session and requireRole('admin'). Pass the individual operator's bearer through to the API instead of ADMIN_API_BEARER so the API's request.currentUser identifies the actor. If a shared-token model must stay short-term, at minimum: use timingSafeEqual for the cookie compare, set short expiry + HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Strict, support a token-rotation list (accept N most-recent tokens) for zero-downtime rotation, and log a stable operator id separately.

findings.title: GAUSHALA_MANAGER portal has NO IDOR — all gaushala-portal API routes correctly scope by currentUser.id with ownership checks (no vulnerability; documented for completeness)
findings.evidence: gaushala-portal.ts:20-34 GET /donations `if (!roles.includes('GAUSHALA_MANAGER')) return 403; ... const where = { gaushalaId: userId, ... }` (userId = request.currentUser!.id). :55-101 GET /dashboard scopes `gaushalaId: userId` and `findUnique({ where: { userId } })` for the profile. :130-157 PATCH /profile uses `findUnique({ where: { userId } })` / `update({ where: { userId } })`. gaushala-cows.ts:76-126 GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE /cows/:id all do `const existing = await prisma.cow.findFirst({ where: { id, gaushalaId: gaushalaUserId } })` before any update/delete (gaushalaUserId = currentUser.id). gaushala-volunteers.ts:50-70 PATCH/DELETE /volunteers/:id same pattern: `findFirst({ where: { id, gaushalaId: gaushalaUserId } })` then update/delete. Web portal gated by gaushala-portal/layout.tsx AuthGuard allowedRoles ['gaushala_manager'] and pages send `Authorization: Bearer ${session?.accessToken}` (verified gaushala-portal/cows/page.tsx).
findings.impact: Manager A cannot read or mutate manager B's gaushala profile, donations, cows, or volunteers — every query is filtered by gaushalaId = currentUser.id and every by-id mutation is preceded by an ownership findFirst. This is the correct pattern and contrasts sharply with the vulnerable temple-portal /schedule (B1). No privilege escalation or IDOR found in the gaushala domain.
findings.repro: N/A — no vulnerability. (Negative result recorded so the coverage claim 'gaushala IDOR checked' is auditable.)
findings.suggestedFix: No change required. Recommend applying this same resolve-by-currentUser + ownership-findFirst pattern to temple-portal /schedule to fix B1.

findings.title: All apps/api admin*.ts routes verified to carry requireRole('admin') — no missing-guard privilege escalation found (negative result; documented for completeness)
findings.evidence: Checked every listed admin route file for preHandler [authenticateUser, requireRole('admin')] (or token-gated cron equivalents): admin.ts, admin-ops.ts (GET ops routes use authorisedToken CRON_AUTH_TOKEN; POST /sla-overdue-bookings/resolve uses [authenticateUser, requireRole('admin')]), admin-queue.ts, admin-metrics.ts (authorised() = token OR admin-Bearer), admin-leads.ts (adminPreHandlers on all incl. PATCH /leads/:id/status, POST /leads/import, GET /cron/tick token-gated with timing-safe compare + header-preferred token), admin-roadmap.ts (`{ preHandler: [authenticateUser, requireRole('admin')] }`), admin-subscriptions.ts, admin-agents.ts (path-traversal protected: `/^[\w\-\d]+\.md$/` regex + `fpath.startsWith(REPORT_DIR)`), admin-gurukuls.ts, admin-lead-conversion.ts, admin-bookings.ts (adminPreHandlers on payouts/refunds/post actions), admin-temples.ts, admin-content-queue.ts (adminPreHandlers on all incl. /run, /auto-post, /generate), admin-donations-export.ts ([authenticateUser, requireRole('admin')]), marketplace-v2 marketplaceAdminRoutes (/keys POST/GET/DELETE all adminPreHandlers), outreach-webhook outreachAdminRoutes (/run /logs /config adminPreHandlers), whatsapp-broadcast whatsappBroadcastRoutes (adminPreHandlers). The only admin-namespaced routes NOT behind requireRole('admin') are token-gated cron/agent endpoints (admin-ops GETs, admin-metrics, admin-roadmap-orchestrator X-Orchestrator-Secret, admin-leads /cron/tick) which is the intended shared-secret model for GH-Actions callers.
findings.impact: No privilege-escalation via a missing admin guard on the API. A non-admin JWT cannot reach any admin data-mutation route. The residual admin-surface weaknesses are the client-side-only web gating (B3) and the shared-token/no-per-user-identity model (B4), not missing API guards.
findings.suggestedFix: No change required for the API guards. Note for hardening: the cron token-gated GETs (admin-ops, admin-metrics, admin-leads /cron/tick) accept the token via ?token= query (legacy) which can leak into Render access logs / CDN caches — admin-leads /cron/tick already prefers the x-cron-token header (P0 hardening comment); apply the same header-preferred pattern to admin-ops and admin-metrics token reads to keep the secret out of URLs.

findings.title: Self-escalation check: PATCH /admin/users/:id role changes require admin and cannot be self-targeted to escalate — no self-escalation path found (negative result)
findings.evidence: admin-api.ts patchUser: `export async function patchUser(token, userId, updates: { approved?, blocked?, roles?: BackendRole[] }) { const res = await fetch(`${API_BASE_URL}/admin/users/${userId}`, { method: 'PATCH', headers: { 'Content-Type':'application/json', ...authHeaders(token) }, body: JSON.stringify(updates) }) }` — always sends the caller's Bearer token. The receiving admin route requires [authenticateUser, requireRole('admin')], so a non-admin's token is 403'd before any role write. The users page (apps/web/app/admin/users/page.tsx) is wrapped by the admin layout's AuthGuard(['admin']) and only renders the role-change UI to admins. No endpoint allows a user to patch their OWN roles without already being admin (the guard precedes the mutation).
findings.impact: A regular DEVOTEE/PANDIT/etc. cannot make themselves ADMIN: the role-change endpoint is admin-gated and the client that exposes it is itself admin-gated (client-side). There is no unauthenticated or self-targeted role-write path. (Caveat: the client-side gating in B3 means the role-change UI is *reachable* by a non-admin, but the actual mutation still requires a valid admin JWT on the API, so escalation does not succeed.)
findings.suggestedFix: No change required beyond fixing B3 (so the role-change UI is not even rendered for non-admins). Additionally, consider an explicit server-side guard in the PATCH /admin/users/:id handler that forbids a user from modifying their own roles (defense-in-depth against a compromised admin locking in their own privilege), and log every role change with the actor identity — which requires B4's per-user bearer to be meaningful.
